newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO not intimidated by Serb retaliation - Clark.
newsitem.headline: NATO not intimidated by Serb retaliation - Clark.

text.p: NATO supreme commander General Wesley Clark said on Friday that Bosnian Serb retaliation for a raid on indicted war criminals would not intimidate the alliance-led peace force.
He made clear during a visit to Sarajevo that the alliance would not shrink from a tougher stance towards suspected war criminals despite a wave of low-level violence in revenge for the NATO swoop.
"We've seen some efforts by some in Srpska (the Serb republic) to intimidate their own people.
"I can tell you NATO is not going to be intimidated by any of this and we are going to follow through on our own mandate," Clark told reporters.

The general indicated the NATO raid last week against two Serb suspects wanted by the United Nations had rattled nationalist leaders loyal to former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic, who is also an indicted war criminal.
"We must be having an impact on Karadzic and the rest of the war criminals there or there would not be a response," he said.
The newly-appointed Supreme Allied Commander met officers in the NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) a week after British soldiers pounced on two suspects in the northwest Prijedor region.

One suspect was seized and extradited to face trail before the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague and another was shot dead after resisting arrest. Both men were charged under sealed indictments with leading "ethnic cleansing" against Moslems and Croats around Prijedor in during the 1992-1995 Bosnian war.
Clark said SFOR's mandate in Bosnia had not changed but the arrest broke new ground for the mission which had previously ruled out going after suspects unless peacekeeping troops stumbled upon them.
Hours before the general's visit, a hand grenade detonated outside the apartment of an international police monitor in Gradiska, 50 km (30 miles) north of Banja Luka in Serb territory.
The police monitor, who was sleeping when the attack occurred early on Friday morning, was not injured in the explosion which shattered windows in his apartment, the United Nations said.

The fifth explosion in as many days was part of a retaliatory campaign targeting international monitors and NATO soldiers. No one has been seriously injured in the incidents and Western officials said they had no plans to evacuate staff.
The explosions have been accompanied by vitriolic attacks in official Serb media against NATO, accusing the West of persecuting the Serb nation.

Posters bearing a portrait of Karadzic were plastered overnight on the offices U.N. and other international agencies across Serb territory. Below Karadzic's picture were the words: "Don't touch him - he means peace".

Diplomats said the threats and minor explosions were part of an attempt by Serb nationalists to test the resolve and unity of Western governments which have often disagreed over how to treat the war crimes issue.

French officials privately complained that the arrest operation was not properly coordinated with diplomatic initiatives. France has denied a New York Times report that said Paris rejected plans to launch a raid around Pale, outside Sarajevo, which serves as headquarters for Karadzic.

The former Sarajevo psyychiatrist has been locked in a power struggle with his former protege, Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic, who has accused him and his allies of robbing state coffers through smuggling rackets.
The suspect shot in the NATO raid, notorious police chief Simo Drljaca, was a loyal servant to Karadzic who posed a potential threat to Plavsic's authority in the northwest Banja Luka region.
